chapters.title: The train arrives
chapters.source: estimated: staging of a typical weekday morning boarding

captions.text: The station is split into paid and unpaid areas, and the fare gates are the only way in.
Tap in with a card or a phone, and the fare runs to the tap out at the end.
Glass screen doors line the track: Singapore's MRT was the first in Asia to use them, back in 1987.
They are full height underground and half height at elevated stations, and by 14 March 2012 every elevated station had them.
Queue to one side of the door, behind the yellow line.
The train arrives, and the platform doors open with it.
The announcement asks you to mind the platform gap, and important MRT announcements are made in four languages.
Then move in, so the people behind you can board.
The doors close, and the MRT carries on: more than 140 stations on six lines, and over three million rides a day.

facts.text: Stations are divided into two areas, paid and unpaid, which collect fares by restricting entry only through the fare gates (access control gates).
Fares are charged based on commuters "tapping in" at the start and "tapping out" at the destination; the failure to tap out generally results in full or flat fare(s).
The Singapore MRT was the first rapid transit system in Asia to incorporate glass platform screen doors, in its underground stations in 1987.
Full-height platform screen doors are installed at all existing underground MRT and sub-surface stations in Singapore; half-height platform screen doors are installed at elevated stations.
By 14 March 2012, all elevated MRT stations had been retrofitted with half-height platform screen doors and were operational.
LTA's Thoughtful Bunch campaign asks commuters to queue to one side of the door and let others alight first.
The same LTA campaign asks commuters to move in to make space so others can board.
On Singapore's MRT, the phrases "Please mind the platform gap" and "Please mind the gap" are used in announcements in English.
In Singapore's MRT, important train announcements are made in the four official languages.
Today more than 140 stations across six MRT lines span the island, a 200 km system with over three million daily ridership, run by SMRT and SBS Transit.
